################################################################
## 11_stack_array.cpp
################################################################
=== 1. the whole data structure in bytes ===
  sizeof(int)=4 sizeof(size_t)=8
  sizeof(ArrayStack<int,5>)  = 40
  sizeof(ArrayStack<char,5>) = 24
  the 5 ints alone           = 20 bytes
  the bookkeeping            = 16 bytes (top index + refusal counter)
  offsetof(data)    = 0
  offsetof(top)     = 24
  offsetof(refusals)= 32
  offsetof(top) = 24, not 20: size_t wants an 8 byte boundary, so 4 bytes of padding sit after the 5 ints
  the array comes first and the index trails it, which is why the base address never moves

=== 2. push and pop operation log (LIFO proof) ===
  push(10) -> ok    topIndex=1 content: 10
  push(20) -> ok    topIndex=2 content: 10 20
  push(30) -> ok    topIndex=3 content: 10 20 30
  inputs were 10 20 30, pops come out in the reverse order:
  pop() -> 30   remaining topIndex=2
  pop() -> 20   remaining topIndex=1
  pop() -> 10   remaining topIndex=0
  after the last pop: empty=yes, pop on empty now returns false (underflow)

=== 3. the three operations in one line each ===
  push(x) : data[top] = x; top++      both O(1), nothing shifts, nothing allocates
  pop()   : top--; return data[top]   O(1)
  top()   : return data[top - 1]      O(1), the stack is not modified

=== 4. the capacity limit is real: 7 pushes into a 5 slot stack ===
  push(1) -> stored   size=1 full=no refusals=0
  push(2) -> stored   size=2 full=no refusals=0
  push(3) -> stored   size=3 full=no refusals=0
  push(4) -> stored   size=4 full=no refusals=0
  push(5) -> stored   size=5 full=yes refusals=0
  push(6) -> REFUSED (full)   size=5 full=yes refusals=1
  push(7) -> REFUSED (full)   size=5 full=yes refusals=2
  after the refusals the contents are untouched: bottom -> top: 1 2 3 4 5   size=5
  refused pushes = 2, capacity() = 5, overflow is DETECTED, not silently written
  drain: 5 4 3 2 1 

=== 5. where an unchecked push would write (address arithmetic) ===
  bench.data base            = 0x7ffeb0a2d3e0
  bench.data + 6*sizeof(int) = 0x7ffeb0a2d3f8
  address of bench.canary    = 0x7ffeb0a2d3f8
  the unchecked slot 6 IS the canary slot: yes
  canary before = 0xc0ffee (that is the byte a stack with no full() check would overwrite)
  offsetof(CanaryBench,canary) = 24 bytes, exactly 6 ints in

=== 6. cost: 2,000,000 pushes then 2,000,000 pops ===
  the container itself asked the heap for 1 block of 8000016 bytes for a 8000016 byte object
  the 2,000,000 pushes and 2,000,000 pops asked the heap for 0 further blocks and 0 further bytes
  the popped values sum to 1999999000000 against 1999999000000 if every value came back in reverse: confirmed
  per operation: push 0.688 ns, pop 0.378 ns
  refusals at the end = 0

=== 6b. why the TOP end and not the BOTTOM end ===
  bottom end (every push shifts the whole stack): 484.7 ns per push
  top end    (nothing shifts)                    : 0.1 ns per push
  the bottom end costs 4267.2x more for the SAME 20,000 pushes
  both loops end in a checksum (399980000) so the compiler cannot delete the work
  (the gap grows with n, which is the whole argument for choosing the end)

=== 7. the one line to remember ===
  a stack is an array plus one index; push stores at the index and moves it,
  pop moves it back and returns the slot. O(1) both, zero allocation after the array exists.
## exit code: 0

################################################################
## 12_stack_linked_apps.cpp
################################################################
=== 1. the node and the stack in bytes ===
  sizeof(Node{int data; Node *next;}) = 16  offsetof(data)=0 offsetof(next)=8
  4 payload bytes + 4 padding bytes + 8 pointer bytes = 16, the padding exists so the
  pointer sits on an 8 byte boundary (lecture 5 measured the same rule)
  sizeof(LinkedStack) = 24 bytes: one pointer, one count, one counter
  so the stack object itself is constant size and every element lives on the heap

=== 2. push log: the newest node becomes the head ===
  push(10)  new node at 0x5aaba91d1030 -> head_ now points here, head_->data=10, head_->next=0, size=1
  push(20)  new node at 0x5aaba91d1050 -> head_ now points here, head_->data=20, head_->next=0x5aaba91d1030, size=2
  push(30)  new node at 0x5aaba91d1070 -> head_ now points here, head_->data=30, head_->next=0x5aaba91d1050, size=3
  the head moved every time: LIFO is head insertion, nothing is traversed to push

=== 3. pop log and the real underflow failure ===
  pop() -> 30  size=2  head=0x5aaba91d1050
  pop() -> 20  size=1  head=0x5aaba91d1030
  pop() -> 10  size=0  head=0
  pop() on an empty stack returned false, underflow counter = 2 (the drain loop's last attempt plus this one)
  a linked stack cannot overflow, it can only underflow: the two failure modes are not symmetric

=== 4. no capacity limit: 200,000 pushes ===
  pushed 200000 elements with 200000 heap requests requesting 3200000 bytes, which is 16 bytes per element
  the allocator hands out 24 usable bytes per node and charges a 32 byte stride, so the real footprint is 6400000 bytes for the 3200000 bytes asked for
  no full() check exists anywhere: the limit is the machine's memory, not the container
  draining 200000 nodes made 200000 free calls, underflows = 1

=== 5. the trade in one table, measured ===
  property                  array stack (lecture 11)  linked stack
  heap calls per element    0                         1
  bytes charged per element 4                         32
  capacity limit            fixed at compile time     none
  overflow possible         yes, detected             no
  underflow possible        yes, detected             yes, detected
  push/pop work             O(1)                      O(1)
  locality                  contiguous, cache friendly scattered, pointer chase

=== 6. application 1: balanced bracket checker ===
  "(a[b]{c})"  -> BALANCED  (all pairs matched)
  "([)]"  -> NOT BALANCED  (expected ( but found ) at index 2)
  "((("  -> NOT BALANCED  (never closed, the deepest unmatched opener is ( at index 2)
  ")("  -> NOT BALANCED  (closing ) with nothing open at index 0)
  "{[()]}"  -> BALANCED  (all pairs matched)
  ""  -> BALANCED  (all pairs matched)
  the stack is what makes this O(n): an opened bracket is pushed, a closing bracket must
  match the TOP. A counter would pass "([)]", a stack catches it at index 2. Trace of that case:
    push ( at 0  depth=1
    push [ at 1  depth=2
    hit ) at 2 while top is [ -> fail

=== 7. application 2: reverse a string with the stack ===
  "DSA" -> "ASD"   palindrome=no
  "ECE2104" -> "4012ECE"   palindrome=no
  "level" -> "level"   palindrome=yes
  reversing is push everything then pop everything: the LIFO rule IS the reversal

=== 8. cost of the two representations, timed in this one process ===
  order verified by checksum: linked ok, array ok (the checksum is what stops the compiler deleting the loops)
  linked stack: push 16.027 ns, pop 8.330 ns, 1000000 heap requests for 1,000,000 elements
  array stack : push 0.639 ns, pop 0.323 ns, 1 heap request of 4000008 bytes, storage 4000000 bytes
  the linked stack pays 25.8x more per pop, and that is the allocator: the array stack never asked it
  for anything after the single block was reserved
  what it bought: no ceiling. Choose the array when the bound is known, the links when it is not.

=== 9. the one line to remember ===
  a linked stack is head insertion plus head removal; the top of the stack is the head pointer,
  which is why push and pop are O(1) with no shifting and why the stack has no capacity
## exit code: 0

################################################################
## 13_queue_array.cpp
################################################################
=== 1. the queue is two indices plus its array ===
  sizeof(int)=4
  sizeof(NaiveQueue<int,5>)    = 48
  sizeof(CircularQueue<int,5>) = 64
  the array is 20 bytes, the bookkeeping is 24 bytes in the naive form and 40 in the circular form
  enqueue writes at rear, then rear++   (one end)
  dequeue reads at front, then front++  (the OTHER end)

=== 2. FIFO proof: enqueue 10 20 30, dequeue three times ===
  enqueue(10)  rearIndex=1 size=1
  enqueue(20)  rearIndex=2 size=2
  enqueue(30)  rearIndex=3 size=3
  dequeue() -> 10  frontIndex=1 size=2
  dequeue() -> 20  frontIndex=2 size=1
  dequeue() -> 30  frontIndex=3 size=0
  inputs were 10 20 30 and they came back 10 20 30: same order, opposite of the stack
  a queue is what a printer does with its jobs and what a scheduler does with processes

=== 3. operation log with the indices that matter ===
  after 5 enqueues: frontIndex=0 rearIndex=5 size=5 empty=no full=yes  slots: [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
  dequeue() -> 1
  dequeue() -> 2
  dequeue() -> 3
  after 3 dequeues: frontIndex=3 rearIndex=5 size=2 empty=no full=yes  slots: [--] [--] [--] [4] [5]
  free slots BELOW front = 3, free slots at rear = 0, live elements = 2

=== 4. the exact point where the naive queue wastes slots ===
  enqueue(6) -> REFUSED (rear == capacity)   rearIndex=5 size=2 refusals=1
  enqueue(7) -> REFUSED (rear == capacity)   rearIndex=5 size=2 refusals=2
  state at the refusal: frontIndex=3 rearIndex=5 size=2 empty=no full=yes  slots: [--] [--] [--] [4] [5]
  the queue holds 2 elements, index 5 is off the end of the array, and indices 0 to 2 (that is 3 slots) are still valid memory
  the exact operation is enqueue #6 of this sequence: after 5 enqueues and 3 dequeues,
  rear == capacity, so full() says yes while 3 of the 5 slots are unreachable. Space lost = frontIndex = 3 slots.
  drain the rest: 4 5 
  after draining: frontIndex=5 rearIndex=5 size=0 empty=yes full=yes  slots: [--] [--] [--] [--] [--]
  now size=0 but rearIndex=5, and a naive queue that does not reset the indices can never enqueue again:
  dequeue says empty while full() still says full: both true at once

=== 5. the repair in one line, measured on the same sequence ===
  rear = (rear + 1) % capacity   and   front = (front + 1) % capacity
  the same script run on both forms: 5 enqueues, 3 dequeues, then 3 more enqueues
  naive form    : refused 3 of those 3 enqueues, holds 2 elements
  circular form : refused 0 of those 3 enqueues, holds 5 elements
  every dequeue in the circular form frees its slot for exactly the next enqueue

=== 6. cost: 1,000,000 enqueues plus 1,000,000 dequeues ===
  the container asked the heap for 1 block of 4136 bytes (the array lives inside the object)
  the 2,000,000 operations asked the heap for 0 blocks and 0 bytes
  every dequeue returned the value its enqueue put in, in order: yes
  per operation: 1.027 ns, index wraps survived = 976

=== 7. the one line to remember ===
  a naive array queue is correct for at most capacity operations before the front abandons
  the space behind it; making the index wrap (front/rear mod capacity) is what turns a
  one-shot queue into a reusable one, and it costs one modulo per operation.
## exit code: 0

################################################################
## 14_queue_linked_circular.cpp
################################################################
=== 1. the linked queue in bytes ===
  sizeof(QNode{int data; QNode *next;}) = 16  offsetof(data)=0 offsetof(next)=8
  sizeof(LinkedQueue) = 32 bytes (front pointer, rear pointer, count, underflow counter)
  the queue holds TWO ends: enqueue writes through rear_, dequeue reads front_, both O(1)
  a linked queue never says full: it has no capacity to exceed

=== 2. enqueue and dequeue log with real node addresses ===
  enqueue(7)  node at 0x6466e9ca0030  front=0x6466e9ca0030 rear=0x6466e9ca0030 size=1
  enqueue(8)  node at 0x6466e9ca0050  front=0x6466e9ca0030 rear=0x6466e9ca0050 size=2
  enqueue(9)  node at 0x6466e9ca0070  front=0x6466e9ca0030 rear=0x6466e9ca0070 size=3
  the front node stays put while the rear walks away from it: that is the whole queue
  dequeue() -> 7  front now 0x6466e9ca0050 size=2
  dequeue() -> 8  front now 0x6466e9ca0070 size=1
  dequeue() -> 9  front now 0 size=0
  dequeue on empty returns false, underflows=2
  the allocator charges 24 usable bytes per node for the 16 byte request

=== 3. no ceiling: 200,000 enqueues through the linked queue ===
  enqueued 200000 elements with 200000 heap requests requesting 3200000 bytes, and the drain made 200000 free calls
  cost: one 16 byte node per element and a pointer per hop, in exchange for no limit

=== 4. circular queue: the index trajectory through TWO wrap-arounds ===
  capacity = 5, the script is enqueue enqueue dequeue dequeue, five times over
  op  val   front   rear  count  wraps  note
  enq 100   0       1     1      0      
  enq 101   0       2     2      0      
  deq 100   1       2     1      0      
  deq 101   2       2     0      0      
  enq 102   2       3     1      0      
  enq 103   2       4     2      0      
  deq 102   3       4     1      0      
  deq 103   4       4     0      0      
  enq 104   4       0     1      1        <- rear wrapped past the end of the array
  enq 105   4       1     2      1      
  deq 104   0       1     1      1      
  deq 105   1       1     0      1      
  enq 106   1       2     1      1      
  enq 107   1       3     2      1      
  deq 106   2       3     1      1      
  deq 107   3       3     0      1      
  enq 108   3       4     1      1      
  enq 109   3       0     2      2        <- rear wrapped past the end of the array
  deq 108   4       0     1      2      
  deq 109   0       0     0      2      
  10 enqueues into a 5 slot array and the rear index came round 2 times: the same 5 slots served all of them
  a naive queue would have refused after 5 enqueues: this one is still running

=== 5. the count formula, evaluated on the states above ===
  count = (rear - front + capacity) mod capacity
  state A: front=0 rear=3 -> formula = (3 - 0 + 5) mod 5 = 3 and the stored count is 3
  state B: front=2 rear=3 -> formula = (3 - 2 + 5) mod 5 = 1 and the stored count is 1
  state C (a wrapped one): front=3 rear=2, bare (rear - front) as unsigned = 18446744073709551615
    while the formula gives (2 - 3 + 5) mod 5 = 4 and the stored count is 4
  that wrapped number is the whole reason the + capacity sits in the formula

=== 6. full/empty ambiguity and the two ways out ===
  front == rear means EMPTY in the count-free design, and it is also what you get after
  capacity enqueues (rear caught up with front again), so one comparison cannot decide both.
  count based: front=3 rear=3 count=0 -> empty, decided by the count
  sentinel slot: after 4 enqueues usable=4 front=0 rear=4 full=yes refusals=0
  the sentinel design pays one slot of the array to keep the test to one comparison:
  it stores 4 of 5 slots, the count design stores all 5

=== 7. cost of the three queue shapes, timed in this one process ===
  fifo order verified in both loops: yes
  linked queue  : 14.023 ns per operation, 1000000 heap requests (one node per element, freed on the way out)
  circular queue: 0.531 ns per operation, 0 heap requests during the operations (the array is inside the object)
  the linked queue is 26.42x slower per operation: that gap is the allocator, not the pointer arithmetic
  the circular queue pays one modulo per operation instead, and it needs a known capacity

=== 8. the one line to remember ===
  rear = (rear + 1) mod capacity turns the array into a ring; the queue stops wasting the
  space behind the front, and count = (rear - front + capacity) mod capacity tells you how
  many elements are inside it
## exit code: 0

################################################################
## 15_queue_apps.cpp
################################################################
=== 1. what a queue gives you ===
  first in, first out: the element that has waited longest leaves first
  that single rule is the scheduler, the printer spooler, the keyboard buffer, and BFS

=== 2. round robin scheduling over 5 tasks (quantum = 3) ===
  start end  task  ran       remaining  state
  0     3    A     3         5          back to the tail of the queue
  3     6    B     3         1          back to the tail of the queue
  6     9    C     3         6          back to the tail of the queue
  9     11   D     2         0          DONE
  11    14   E     3         3          back to the tail of the queue
  14    17   A     3         2          back to the tail of the queue
  17    18   B     1         0          DONE
  18    21   C     3         3          back to the tail of the queue
  21    24   E     3         0          DONE
  24    26   A     2         0          DONE
  26    29   C     3         0          DONE
  completion order: D B E A C
  total time = 29, slices = 11 (one context switch per slice)
  round robin: average waiting = 15.80, average turnaround = 21.60, worst waiting = 20

=== 3. the same five tasks served first come first served ===
  start end  task  burst     waiting
  0     8    A     8         0
  8     12   B     4         8
  12    21   C     9         12
  21    23   D     2         21
  23    29   E     6         23
  FCFS: average waiting = 12.80, average turnaround = 18.60, worst waiting = 23
  measured trade: worst wait is 20 under round robin against 23 under FCFS, so RR wins there by 3 time units
  and it loses 3.00 on the average wait. Nobody starves under RR; the average pays for it.

=== 4. a queue built from two stacks ===
  enqueue pushes onto the IN stack, dequeue pops from the OUT stack.
  when OUT is empty, everything is poured from IN to OUT, which reverses it twice, so
  the oldest element ends up on top of OUT. That is the FIFO order, made out of LIFO parts.
  op      value transfers   size    note
  enqueue 10    0           1       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  enqueue 20    0           2       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  enqueue 30    0           3       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  enqueue 40    0           4       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  enqueue 50    0           5       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  enqueue 60    0           6       pushed onto IN, no transfer yet
  dequeue 10    6           5       one bulk transfer of 6, then plain pops
  dequeue 20    6           4       
  dequeue 30    6           3       
  dequeue 40    6           2       
  dequeue 50    6           1       
  dequeue 60    6           0       
  order check: enqueued 10 20 30 40 50 60 and they came back in that order: yes
  total transfers for 6 elements = 6: each element moved from IN to OUT exactly once,
  so a dequeue costs 1 pop on average even though the worst single one cost 6

=== 5. queue from two stacks against std::queue on the same operation stream ===
  200 mixed operations, followed by a full drain
  the two-stack queue returned the same values in the same order as std::queue: yes
  transfers over the whole run = 138 for 138 enqueues and 200 operations
  each element is poured from IN to OUT at most once, so transfers <= enqueues: yes

=== 6. the reverse trick: a stack from two queues ===
  push into the queue, then rotate the other n-1 elements behind it so it sits at the front
  push(1)  rotations so far = 0  (that push cost 0 rotations)
  push(2)  rotations so far = 1  (that push cost 1 rotations)
  push(3)  rotations so far = 3  (that push cost 2 rotations)
  push(4)  rotations so far = 6  (that push cost 3 rotations)
  push(5)  rotations so far = 10  (that push cost 4 rotations)
  push(6)  rotations so far = 15  (that push cost 5 rotations)
  pops come back: 6 5 4 3 2 1
  LIFO recovered out of two FIFO queues, but look at the price: the same 6 pushes cost 15 rotations,
  which is 1 + 2 + ... + 5 = 15. A push is O(n) here against O(1) for a real stack: the trick works, it just is not free.

=== 7. cost of the two-stack queue, timed ===
  500000 enqueues and 500000 dequeues, every dequeue immediately after its enqueue
  so the transfer happens on every single dequeue: 1.190 ns per operation, transfers = 500000, order verified: yes
  (that pattern IS the worst case for the two-stack design; a real workload batches, and
   the measured 6 element run above shows the good case: 1 transfer per element in total)

=== 8. the one line to remember ===
  a queue is the shape of anything that must serve arrival order, and any structure that
  can reverse a sequence twice can imitate it. Check the cost: round robin pays in average
  waiting, the two-stack queue pays in transfers, both own their place
## exit code: 0
